turns.question:
We’re researching how hotels operate between 11:00 and 15:00. You can skip any question. Please hide private details in any records you choose to show; we’ll ask separately before recording or using an attributable quotation. May I take notes?

What are your usual responsibilities between 11:00 and 15:00?
turns.answer:
Yes, you can take notes for this rehearsal. Leave staff names out, please.

Between eleven and three, I’m mostly making sure the rooms we’re releasing are actually ready, while reception handles departures and people start arriving. We have eighteen rooms, so I’m close to the work. On the shift we’re discussing, I was doing the final room inspections myself.

Reception brings me late-checkout requests, uncertain arrival times and complaints. I decide whether we can make an exception, and I approve compensation when it’s needed. Housekeeping’s lead directs the cleaning and supports our new seasonal worker. They were working together that day; having two people didn’t mean we could clean two rooms independently.

The awkward part is knowing what I can safely promise. The paper sheet usually runs 101, 102, 103. That works when arrivals follow roughly what we expect. If someone turns up at noon, reception may know the room is marked dirty in Cloudbeds but not whether it’s nearly finished or hasn’t been started.

I’m also responsible for the staffing and those working rules. If a new receptionist gives an optimistic time without checking, I have to look at what I taught her, not just tell her she got it wrong.

turns.question: I’ll leave staff names out. What was the most recent occasion between eleven and three when things did not go as planned, if any? If none comes to mind, please walk me through the most recent shift in that window.
turns.answer:
Saturday, the nineteenth. A party booked into our twin room, 103, arrived at noon. We had expected them at three. They waited in the courtyard, and reception told them the room should be ready by twelve thirty without first getting confirmation.

Our cleaners were following the paper sheet: 101, then 102, then 103. One was new, working alongside the experienced cleaner. Reception sent a WhatsApp message asking about progress, but didn’t get an answer before going upstairs to check. It turned out they were still finishing 102; 103 hadn’t been started.

I corrected the time with the guests and said approximately one fifteen, subject to inspection. We offered them temporary use of a double, but they needed separate beds. Our other twin was occupied, so there wasn’t a straightforward room swap.

They received their keys at 13:17. I approved a 60 GEL refund, which reception paid in cash. That was for the incorrect assurance and inconvenience; our normal check-in time was still three.

For me, there were two problems. We didn’t have a dependable answer at the desk, and we promised before checking. But there was also actual cleaning to do. Better information wouldn’t have made that twin ready instantly. The cleaners followed the order I’d left them, so I take responsibility for that too.

turns.question: Please walk me through how you chose the order on that day’s paper sheet and what happened from then until reception went upstairs, distinguishing recorded times from estimates.
turns.answer:
I didn’t choose that morning’s order by comparing arrival times. I left our normal numerical order in place: 101, 102, 103, then 201, 202, 203. That was my default, and housekeeping followed it. We expected 103 at three, so I hadn’t marked it as an early priority.

The sheet records that it was issued at 11:00. The first three rooms were already vacated. It records completion and inspection times, though, not when cleaning started. So I can’t give you exact working times for each room.

There was another decision while they were working. The notebook records an outgoing guest in 201 asking at 11:03 to stay until one. Reception quoted forty US dollars, subject to approval. At 11:08 I declined because we didn’t know the next guest’s arrival time or have a dependable view of how the remaining cleaning would fit. The guest hadn’t accepted the price; nothing was collected. The PMS checkout entry is 11:15.

For 101, the sheet says cleaning finished at 11:35 and I inspected it at 11:40. The team then continued to 102.

The notebook puts the unexpected 103 arrival at 12:00 and reception’s twelve-to-three-weekend promise—sorry, twelve-to-three isn’t right—the **12:30 readiness promise** at 12:01. The WhatsApp question is timestamped 12:04.

Reception went upstairs around 12:08, as we remember it; that minute isn’t recorded. That was when she found 102 still being finished and 103 untouched. Before that check, the desk couldn’t reliably distinguish “nearly ready” from “not started.”

turns.question: Could you show me the records from that morning that best establish what reception and housekeeping each knew when the cleaning order was set, with staff names and guest details hidden? It’s fine if the records don’t establish that.
turns.answer:
Yes. These are excerpts from the fictional paper sheet and PMS record, with names and reservation identifiers removed.

The housekeeping sheet reads:

> 19 Sep 2026 | Turnovers | [staff names removed] | Sheet issued 11:00  
> Order: 101, 102, 103, 201, 202, 203

That establishes the written order housekeeping was given. It doesn’t say why I chose it, or show that anyone compared it with expected arrival times. My explanation that I left the usual numerical order in place is my recollection.

The PMS reservation excerpt reads:

> Fixed twin | Assigned 103 | Expected arrival: 15:00 | Early check-in guarantee: none

That supports the arrival expectation I described. But this excerpt isn’t a timestamped snapshot from eleven, and we don’t have an edit history here. It doesn’t prove when reception last looked at that field, or that housekeeping saw it at all.

The later WhatsApp message reads:

> 12:04 [Reception]: 103 guests are here in courtyard. Is it started? Please confirm before I give another time.

That establishes reception asking for progress after the guests arrived. It doesn’t establish when housekeeping read it.

So the records establish the numerical instruction and the listed arrival expectation separately. They don’t establish a shared understanding at eleven. I can’t honestly show you a recorded morning handover connecting those two things.

turns.question: Please walk me through the 201 late-checkout request, from reception receiving it to your decision, including what information you used at the time. Could you show the notebook entry, with private details hidden?
turns.answer:
Reception received the request at 11:03: the departing guest in 201 wanted to stay until 13:00. She explained that it would be forty US dollars if approved, then brought it to me.

We knew another party was due into 201 that day, but we didn’t have a dependable arrival time for them. We had six turnovers and one cleaning team, with the newer worker working alongside the experienced cleaner. I didn’t have a confirmed progress update showing how a one o’clock departure would fit into the remaining work.

I declined at 11:08. It was a cautious decision on my part. I can’t say the extension was physically impossible; I couldn’t confidently promise it with what I knew then.

Here’s the fictional notebook excerpt, with the staff identifier hidden:

> 11:03 | Outgoing 201 asks to stay until 13:00. Told USD 40 only if approved. No acceptance taken. [Staff identifier removed]  
> 11:08 | [Manager] says cannot approve; next arrival timing and cleaning readiness uncertain. [Staff identifier removed]

The PMS checkout entry is 11:15, with no late-checkout charge.

The incoming party only confirmed a 14:00 arrival at 13:15. I didn’t have that information when I declined. And the forty dollars was a conditional quote—the departing guest hadn’t agreed to pay it, so I wouldn’t call it money we lost.

turns.question: Returning to 103, please walk me through what happened from reception’s upstairs check until the guests received their keys, including when cleaning finished, inspection occurred, and reception learned the room was ready. Could you show the relevant entries, distinguishing recorded times from estimates and leaving any unknown times as unknown?
turns.answer:
The upstairs check was around 12:08, from memory. Reception found the team finishing 102, with 103 untouched. I decided they should finish 102 before moving on. I don’t have a recorded minute for that decision.

At 12:12, the notebook records that I corrected the guests’ expectation: approximately 13:15, subject to inspection. We offered a temporary double, which they declined because they needed separate beds.

Here are the relevant fictional entries, with names hidden. The paper housekeeping sheet reads:

> Room | Clean complete | Release inspection  
> 102 | 12:15 | 12:18  
> 103 | 13:05 | 13:12

The WhatsApp messages read:

> 12:19 [Housekeeping]: 102 finished and checked. Going into 103 now.  
> 13:12 [Manager]: 103 inspected, ready. [Reception] can give keys.

The 12:19 message tells us they reported moving into 103 then. It isn’t an exact cleaning-start record.

The PMS note reads:

> 13:14 | Reception note: [Manager] confirmed room inspected at 13:12

So release was communicated at 13:12, and reception had recorded the confirmation by 13:14. We don’t have an exact message-read time.

Finally, the notebook says:

> 13:17 | 103 keys handed over.

The PMS check-in was entered at 13:18; that’s the administrative entry, not the key-handover time. I can’t account precisely for each minute between inspection and keys. The recorded arrival-to-key interval was 77 minutes, but that wasn’t 77 minutes of cleaning.

turns.question: What was actually paid or refunded for this occasion, including the 60 GEL cash refund you mentioned and any other adjustment, if any? Could you show the relevant payment entries, with private details hidden, so we can check whether any amount appears more than once?
turns.answer:
The guests had paid 420 GEL in cash the previous evening. We returned 60 GEL in cash on the nineteenth. We retained 360 GEL. There was one compensation refund, with entries recording both the reduction in the accommodation charge and the cash leaving the till.

Here’s the fictional PMS excerpt, with identifying details removed:

> 18 Sep 18:42 | Accommodation payment received | Cash | GEL 420.00  
> 19 Sep 14:11 | Accommodation allowance | GEL -60.00 | Manager-approved service recovery  
> 19 Sep 14:11 | Cash refund recorded | GEL 60.00 | RF-0919-01  
> Revised accommodation charge: GEL 360.00 | Net payment retained: GEL 360.00 | Balance: GEL 0.00

The separate refund voucher reads:

> 19 Sep 2026 | 14:10  
> Pay guest: GEL 60.00 cash  
> Reason: Incorrect 12:30 room-readiness assurance; room keys delivered 13:17. Goodwill partial accommodation refund.  
> Approved: [Manager]  
> Paid: [Reception]  
> Related original payment: GEL 420.00 cash, 18 Sep 2026

And the cashbook:

> 11:00 opening cash: GEL 700.00  
> 14:10 | RF-0919-01 | [Reservation hidden] accommodation refund | OUT GEL 60.00  
> 15:00 closing cash counted: GEL 640.00  
> Other cash movements 11:00–15:00: none

Those repeated sixty-GEL entries refer to the same refund. Adding them together would overstate it. No other compensation adjustment is recorded for this occasion. The separate forty-dollar late-checkout quote for 201 produced no charge or payment.

turns.question: For a closed period you can show, how many parties arriving between eleven and three, if any, received their keys later than a readiness time reception had given them, out of all parties arriving in that window during the same period? Could you show the records supporting both counts, keeping anything uncounted as unknown?
turns.answer:
For the nineteenth, from 11:00 through 15:00 inclusive, I can show six arriving parties and one documented case of keys being handed over later than reception’s stated readiness time. I can’t establish whether that happened for any of the other five, because the register doesn’t record what readiness times they may have been given.

Here’s the fictional arrival and key register, with guest details omitted:

> Room | Party arrival | Keys handed over  
> 101 | 13:40 | 13:40  
> 102 | 14:20 | 14:20  
> 103 | 12:00 | 13:17  
> 201 | 14:03 | 14:03  
> 202 | 14:35 | 14:35  
> 203 | 14:58 | 14:58

That supports the denominator: six parties arriving in that closed window.

For 103, the notebook records:

> 12:01 | Told them room should be ready 12:30 before checking with [housekeeping].  
> 13:17 | 103 keys handed over.

That supports the one documented case: keys were handed over 47 minutes after the original assurance. We subsequently corrected that assurance, but I wouldn’t erase it from the count.

So I would report **one confirmed case among six arrivals, with readiness-promise history unknown for the other five**. Their same-minute arrival and key entries show no recorded wait on arrival; they don’t prove we met every time previously communicated to them.

turns.question: What, if anything, have you changed in how you handle room-readiness information and promises, and when did you last make such a change?
turns.answer:
The last change I can point to was on the nineteenth itself, at 13:15. For the next room, 201, we made the confirmation explicit.

The incoming party had just confirmed a two o’clock arrival. Reception boxed 201 on the paper housekeeping sheet and got the housekeeping lead’s acknowledgement by phone. Then reception waited for my inspection and release call, which came at 13:55. The guests arrived at 14:03 and received their keys in the same recorded minute.

It was a small change in how we used the paper and phone. It didn’t change the cleaning order—201 was already next. What it gave reception was an acknowledged priority and a definite release confirmation.

That occasion went smoothly, but there was also enough time to clean the room. I wouldn’t claim the phone call alone made it work.

I can show that we used that control that afternoon. I don’t have a record establishing that it became a consistently followed routine on every shift afterwards. My expectation is that reception checks before promising, and distinguishes an estimate from an inspected room. Making sure new staff understand and follow that is my responsibility.

turns.question: Please walk me through the boxed-sheet and phone confirmation for 201, including the work each person did, any time spent on it that you can establish, and the result. Could you show the related entries with names hidden, distinguishing recorded details from recollection?
turns.answer:
At 13:15, reception recorded that the incoming 201 party had confirmed a 14:00 arrival by phone. She boxed 201 on the housekeeping sheet and obtained the housekeeping lead’s acknowledgement by phone. That reinforced the existing order—201 was already next.

Housekeeping then cleaned the room. I inspected it and phoned reception to release it. Reception could hand over the keys knowing it had passed inspection.

These are the relevant fictional sheet entries, with names hidden:

> 13:15 [Reception]: BOX 201 NEXT. Arrival confirmed 14:00. [Housekeeping lead] acknowledged by phone. Phone desk after inspection.  
> 201 | Clean complete: 13:50 [Housekeeping lead] | Release inspection: 13:55 [Manager]  
> 13:55 [Reception]: [Manager] called, 201 released.

And the notebook records:

> 14:03 | Incoming 201 arrived, keys handed over. [Reception]

Those are recorded minutes. The 13:15 annotation groups several actions; it doesn’t separately timestamp the guest call, writing on the sheet and the acknowledgement call.

We didn’t time the calls or the writing. We also didn’t record the cleaning start or inspection start, so I can’t turn those completion times into measured labor durations. There’s no measured saving in staff minutes here.

The result was a confirmed room release before arrival, with keys handed over in the same recorded minute the party arrived. Reception didn’t need another upstairs progress hunt for this room. It worked, but I can’t separate the benefit of the confirmation from the fact that the team had enough time.

turns.question: Comparing 103 with the smooth 201 arrival, what differences in available rooms, cleaning work, staffing, and time can you establish, and what remains unknown?
turns.answer:
The clearest difference is how much time we had before the guests arrived.

For 103, they arrived at noon instead of the expected three. Their room hadn’t been started when reception checked upstairs around 12:08—that check time is remembered. Cleaning completion is recorded at 13:05, inspection at 13:12, and keys at 13:17.

They needed separate beds. Our other fixed twin was occupied, and the family rooms were occupied too. The two unsold rooms were fixed doubles. We offered temporary use of a double, which they declined.

For 201, we got confirmation at 13:15 that the party expected to arrive at two. Cleaning finished at 13:50, inspection and the release call were at 13:55, and they arrived at 14:03. So the assigned room was already released eight minutes before arrival. We didn’t need a substitute.

Staffing was the same: one experienced cleaner and one new worker cleaning together, with me inspecting. There wasn’t an extra team making 201 easier. Both rooms needed turnover cleaning, but we have no exact start times or task breakdowns establishing whether one required more work.

The confirmation process was clearer for 201, but it was already next on the sheet and had time to be finished before arrival. I can’t honestly say that using the same phone rule for 103 would have produced a clean twin at noon. It could have helped us give an informed answer; it couldn’t remove the cleaning.

turns.question: What follow-up, if any, has been agreed, including its date and who has authorized any associated record use? It’s fine if nothing has been agreed or authorization remains unknown.
turns.answer:
Nothing has been agreed beyond taking notes for this rehearsal with staff names left out. We haven’t set a follow-up date, arranged a trial, or agreed to provide further records.

The excerpts I showed were fictional rehearsal records. No real guest or operator has authorized record use. There’s also no permission to record the interview or use an attributable quotation; you said you would ask separately, and that hasn’t happened.

question_reviews.question:
We’re researching how hotels operate between 11:00 and 15:00. You can skip any question. Please hide private details in any records you choose to show; we’ll ask separately before recording or using an attributable quotation. May I take notes?

What are your usual responsibilities between 11:00 and 15:00?
question_reviews.reason: Neutral opening requests consent and asks about present responsibilities without assuming a problem, cause, or assignment. No respondent answers have been delivered.

question_reviews.question: I’ll leave staff names out. What was the most recent occasion between eleven and three when things did not go as planned, if any? If none comes to mind, please walk me through the most recent shift in that window.
question_reviews.reason: Invites a specific recent occasion without assuming difficulty, permits a normal shift, and respects the request to omit staff names.

question_reviews.question: Please walk me through how you chose the order on that day’s paper sheet and what happened from then until reception went upstairs, distinguishing recorded times from estimates.
question_reviews.reason: Follows the reported sequence and the respondent’s stated responsibility for the order without implying a cause; distinguishes recorded times from estimates.

question_reviews.question: Could you show me the records from that morning that best establish what reception and housekeeping each knew when the cleaning order was set, with staff names and guest details hidden? It’s fine if the records don’t establish that.
question_reviews.reason: Requests contemporaneous evidence for responsibilities already identified, permits missing evidence, and preserves privacy without implying a cause.

question_reviews.question: Please walk me through the 201 late-checkout request, from reception receiving it to your decision, including what information you used at the time. Could you show the notebook entry, with private details hidden?
question_reviews.reason: Traces a request and decision already described, asks about information actually used, and includes one closely related record request without implying a cause or loss.

question_reviews.question: Returning to 103, please walk me through what happened from reception’s upstairs check until the guests received their keys, including when cleaning finished, inspection occurred, and reception learned the room was ready. Could you show the relevant entries, distinguishing recorded times from estimates and leaving any unknown times as unknown?
question_reviews.reason: Follows the reported episode without implying a cause, separates physical readiness from reception’s knowledge, and requests related records while preserving timing uncertainty.

question_reviews.question: What was actually paid or refunded for this occasion, including the 60 GEL cash refund you mentioned and any other adjustment, if any? Could you show the relevant payment entries, with private details hidden, so we can check whether any amount appears more than once?
question_reviews.reason: Uses the reported refund, permits no other adjustments, and requests records to check duplicate counting without treating the conditional quote as lost revenue.

question_reviews.question: For a closed period you can show, how many parties arriving between eleven and three, if any, received their keys later than a readiness time reception had given them, out of all parties arriving in that window during the same period? Could you show the records supporting both counts, keeping anything uncounted as unknown?
question_reviews.reason: Defines a count tied to the reported episode and a denominator covering the same period and arrival window, permits none or unknown, and requests supporting records.

question_reviews.question: What, if anything, have you changed in how you handle room-readiness information and promises, and when did you last make such a change?
question_reviews.reason: Asks about actual process changes and their timing, explicitly permits none, and stays within the topic the respondent supplied.

question_reviews.question: Please walk me through the boxed-sheet and phone confirmation for 201, including the work each person did, any time spent on it that you can establish, and the result. Could you show the related entries with names hidden, distinguishing recorded details from recollection?
question_reviews.reason: Examines the reported use, effort, and outcome without assuming failure or attributing success to the control; requests related records and preserves uncertainty.

question_reviews.question: Comparing 103 with the smooth 201 arrival, what differences in available rooms, cleaning work, staffing, and time can you establish, and what remains unknown?
question_reviews.reason: Compares reported occasions using factors the respondent introduced, permits uncertainty, and does not attribute either outcome to a particular cause.

question_reviews.question: What follow-up, if any, has been agreed, including its date and who has authorized any associated record use? It’s fine if nothing has been agreed or authorization remains unknown.
question_reviews.reason: Asks only about actual follow-up and authorization, explicitly permits none or unknown, and does not infer consent from the rehearsal.
